code.title: Stack (LIFO) vs queue (FIFO): same items, opposite removal order
code.python:
from collections import deque

items = [1, 2, 3]
print("Input order:" + "".join(" " + str(x) for x in items))

stack = []         # a list is a stack: append / pop work at the end
queue = deque()    # deque removes from the front in O(1)
for x in items:
    stack.append(x)    # goes on top
    queue.append(x)    # goes to the back

out = ""
while stack:
    out += " " + str(stack.pop())        # newest leaves first
print("Stack removes (LIFO):" + out)

out = ""
while queue:
    out += " " + str(queue.popleft())    # oldest leaves first
print("Queue removes (FIFO):" + out)
# Time: O(1) per add/remove. Space: O(N).

followUps:
A deque (double-ended queue, said "deck") is a line where you can add and remove at both ends in O(1). A stack uses one end, a queue uses one end for adding and the other for removing; a deque can do either job.

You need one when both ends matter in the same problem: sliding window maximum (drop expired indices from the front, drop smaller values from the back), 0-1 BFS (cost 0 edges go to the front, cost 1 edges to the back), a palindrome check that compares the two ends, or work-stealing schedulers. Example: with [1,2,3], pollFirst() gives 1 and pollLast() gives 3. In Java use ArrayDeque; every operation is O(1) amortized and the space is O(N).

Every Java thread gets its own call stack, and each method call pushes one frame on it; when the method returns, its frame is popped. That is LIFO: the method called last finishes first.

A frame holds the method's local variables, its operand stack (the scratch area where bytecode like iadd pops two numbers and pushes the sum) and the place to return to. Example: main calls f, which calls g. The stack is main, f, g; g returns first, then f. Objects live on the heap; the frame only holds references to them. If recursion goes too deep, frames fill the thread's stack (commonly about 512 KB to 1 MB) and you get StackOverflowError. Space used is O(depth of calls).

code.title: How ArrayDeque works inside: a circular array that doubles when full
code.python:
buf = [0] * 4      # fixed list, used as a ring
head = 0           # index of the oldest item
size = 0

def grow():
    # copy items in queue order into a list twice as big
    global buf, head
    bigger = [0] * (len(buf) * 2)
    for i in range(size):
        bigger[i] = buf[(head + i) % len(buf)]
    buf = bigger
    head = 0

def offer(x):
    global size
    if size == len(buf):
        grow()                               # full: make a bigger list first
    buf[(head + size) % len(buf)] = x        # % makes the tail wrap around to slot 0
    size += 1

def poll():
    global head, size
    x = buf[head]
    head = (head + 1) % len(buf)             # no shifting: just move head forward
    size -= 1
    return x

for x in range(1, 5):
    offer(x)
print("Capacity 4, offer 1 2 3 4")
a = poll()
b = poll()
print("poll twice: " + str(a) + " " + str(b))
offer(5)
offer(6)
print("offer 5 6: tail wraps to slots 0 and 1, capacity still " + str(len(buf)))
offer(7)
print("offer 7: array was full, capacity grows to " + str(len(buf)))
out = ""
while size > 0:
    out += " " + str(poll())
print("poll the rest:" + out)
# Time: O(1) amortized per offer/poll (a grow costs O(N) but is rare). Space: O(N).

followUps:
Nothing fails: when the internal array is full, ArrayDeque allocates a bigger array, copies the elements into it in queue order and carries on. It is unbounded, so you never see a "queue full" error (only OutOfMemoryError if the heap runs out).

The default capacity is 16. In current JDKs the array doubles while it is small (under 64 slots) and grows by 50% after that; older JDKs always doubled. Example: adding the 17th element copies 16 elements once into a larger array. That one add costs O(N), but because the size grows by a constant factor, the copies add up to O(N) over N adds, so each add is O(1) amortized. The array never shrinks on its own.

The methods with "plain" names throw, and the offer/poll/peek family returns a special value. On an empty ArrayDeque:

Throws NoSuchElementExceptionReturns null
pop(), remove(), removeFirst(), removeLast()poll(), pollFirst(), pollLast()
element(), getFirst(), getLast()peek(), peekFirst(), peekLast()

Trap: int x = dq.poll(); on an empty deque gives a NullPointerException when the null is unboxed. For inserting, add/push throw and offer returns false only on a bounded queue that is full; ArrayDeque is never full, but all of them throw NullPointerException for a null element.

code.title: Valid brackets with a stack, and the four ways a string can fail

followUps:
Push the index of each opener instead of the character, so the stack remembers where every open bracket sits.

  1. Closer at index i with an empty stack, or with a top opener of the wrong type: return i.
  2. End of the string with openers left: return the index at the bottom of the stack, the earliest opener that was never closed (some tools report the top one instead; say which you chose).
  3. Otherwise return -1.
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  if (isOpen(s[i])) st.push(i);
  else if (st.isEmpty() || !match(s[st.pop()], s[i])) return i;
}
return st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peekLast();

Example: "(()]" returns 3; "(()" returns 0. Time O(N), space O(N).

With a wildcard (and only one bracket type) you stop using a stack and instead track the range of how many ( could be open: lo = fewest possible, hi = most possible.

  • (: lo++, hi++
  • ): lo--, hi--
  • *: lo--, hi++ (it may close one, open one, or do nothing)

If hi < 0, there are too many closers even in the best case: invalid. If lo < 0, reset it to 0, because the count can never really be negative. At the end the string is valid when lo == 0.

Example "(*))": (1,1), then (0,2), then (0,1), then (0,0), so it is valid (the star acts as (). Time O(N), space O(1).

code.title: Min stack: store (value, minimum so far) so getMin is O(1)
code.python:
ops = [5, 3, 7, 3, 0, 0, 0]      # a number = push it, 0 = pop
st = []                          # each entry is (value, min_so_far)

for x in ops:
    if x != 0:
        # the min at this height = smaller of x and the min just below
        low = x if not st else min(x, st[-1][1])
        st.append((x, low))
        print("push " + str(x) + " -> min " + str(st[-1][1]))
    else:
        value, _ = st.pop()      # pop needs no repair work:
        low = "none" if not st else str(st[-1][1])   # entry below knows its own min
        print("pop " + str(value) + " -> min " + low)

# Time: O(1) for push, pop and getMin.
# Space: O(N), two numbers per element.

followUps:
popMax() removes the largest value even when it sits in the middle, so the "max so far" pair trick is not enough on its own. There are two standard designs.

  • Two stacks, simple: keep (value, maxSoFar) pairs. For popMax, pop into a buffer until you reach the max, remove it, then push the buffer back. popMax is O(N), the rest O(1).
  • Linked list + sorted map, fast: a doubly linked list holds the stack order, and a TreeMap<value, list of nodes> finds the max. popMax takes the last node stored under lastKey() and unlinks it in O(1). Every operation is O(log N).

Example: push 5, 1, 5. popMax must remove the top-most 5, leaving 5, 1. Space is O(N) in both.

Keep a second structure next to the queue: a deque of "candidates for minimum" whose values go up from front to back. Its front is always the current minimum.

  1. enqueue(x): remove values from the back of the deque while they are greater than x (they can never be the minimum again, because x is smaller and leaves later), then add x at the back.
  2. dequeue(): remove the queue's front; if it equals the deque's front, remove that too.
  3. getMin(): read the deque's front.

Example: enqueue 3, 1, 2 gives deque [1, 2], min 1. Dequeue 3: min still 1. Dequeue 1: deque [2], min 2. Each value enters and leaves the deque once, so all operations are O(1) amortized, space O(N). Use > (not >=) so duplicates are kept.

code.title: Next greater element, counting pushes and pops to show the work is at most 2N
code.python:
a = [2, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]
n = len(a)
pushes = pops = 0
res = [-1] * n          # -1 = no greater value to the right
st = []                 # indices still waiting for an answer

for i in range(n):
    # a[i] is the answer for every smaller value waiting on the stack
    while st and a[st[-1]] < a[i]:
        res[st.pop()] = a[i]
        pops += 1
    st.append(i)        # each index is pushed exactly once
    pushes += 1

print("Input:" + "".join(" " + str(x) for x in a))
print("Next greater:" + "".join(" " + str(x) for x in res))
print("Pushes: " + str(pushes) + ", pops: " + str(pops)
      + ", total " + str(pushes + pops) + " <= 2N = " + str(2 * n))
# Time: O(N) because pops can never exceed pushes. Space: O(N).

followUps:
The pop condition is the test "has this waiting element found its answer?", so it must be exactly the relation the problem asks for.

  • Next strictly greater: pop while a[top] < x. An equal value does not pop, so equal elements keep waiting.
  • Next greater-or-equal: pop while a[top] <= x. An equal value counts as the answer.

Example [2, 2, 3]. Strict: the second 2 does not pop the first, and 3 answers both, giving [3, 3, -1]. Greater-or-equal: the second 2 pops the first, giving [2, 3, -1].

Quick check: test with two equal neighbours such as [2, 2]. If the output for the first 2 is not what the problem statement wants, flip < and <=. The cost stays O(N) time, O(N) space either way.

Walk the array twice in one loop: run i from 0 to 2n - 1 and read a[i % n]. The second lap lets elements near the end "see" the elements at the start, as if the array were glued into a ring.

Push an index only during the first lap (i < n); in the second lap you only pop, so every index still gets one answer.

for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) {
  int x = a[i % n];
  while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] < x) res[st.pop()] = x;
  if (i < n) st.push(i);
}

Example [5, 4, 3]: after lap one nothing is answered; in lap two the 5 pops 3 and 4, so the result is [-1, 5, 5]. Whatever is left on the stack (the maximum values) keeps -1. Time O(2N) = O(N), space O(N).

code.title: The four monotonic stack variants: next/previous greater/smaller

followUps:
Yes: one left-to-right pass with an increasing stack gives both, because a pop tells you the "next smaller" of the popped index and the survivor tells you the "previous smaller" of the new index.

  1. Fill next[] with n and prev[] with -1.
  2. For each i: pop while a[top] > a[i] and set next[popped] = i.
  3. Then prev[i] = the top that survived (or -1), and push i.
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] > a[i]) next[st.pop()] = i;
  prev[i] = st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peek();
  st.push(i);
}

Catch: with duplicates, next is strictly smaller but prev is smaller-or-equal. For [2, 2], prev[1] = 0. That is exactly what counting problems want; if you need strict on both sides, skip back over equal values or use two passes. O(N) time and space.

Store indices because an index gives you everything a value gives you, plus the position: you can always read the value back with a[i], but you cannot get a position back from a value.

  • Where to write the answer: when an element is popped you must fill res[thatIndex].
  • Distances and widths: "days until warmer" is i - j; a histogram width is right - left - 1.
  • Duplicates: two 5s are the same value but different indices.
  • Window expiry: a deque must know if its front index has left the window.

Example: temperatures [73, 71, 75]. Day 2 pops index 1 and index 0, and the waits are 2 - 1 = 1 and 2 - 0 = 2. With values 71 and 73 on the stack you could not compute those. Cost is unchanged: O(N) time, O(N) space.

code.title: Largest rectangle in a histogram with an increasing stack and a sentinel

followUps:
Treat every row of the matrix as the ground line of a histogram, and run the histogram solution once per row.

  1. Keep height[j] = number of consecutive 1s ending at the current row in column j.
  2. Moving down one row: a 1 adds one to the column's height, a 0 resets it to 0.
  3. Run Largest Rectangle on height[] and keep the best answer.
for (int[] row : m) {
  for (int j = 0; j < C; j++)
    height[j] = row[j] == 1 ? height[j] + 1 : 0;
  best = Math.max(best, largestRectangle(height));
}

Example rows 1 0 1, 1 1 1, 1 1 1: heights become [1,0,1], [2,1,2], [3,2,3]; the last row gives area 6 (height 2 × width 3). Time O(R × C), extra space O(C).

You need long whenever the largest possible height times the largest possible width can pass 231 − 1, which is about 2.1 × 109.

Check the limits before coding. With heights up to 104 and N up to 105 (the usual LeetCode limits) the worst area is 109, which just fits in an int. With heights up to 109 and N up to 105 the worst area is 1014, which does not fit.

The cast must happen before the multiplication:

long area = (long) h * width;   // correct
long bad  = h * width;          // overflows as int first

The second line multiplies two ints, wraps around silently (Java does not throw), and only then widens. Example: 100000 × 100000 gives 1410065408 instead of 1010.

code.title: Queue from two stacks, counting stack operations to show amortized O(1)
code.python:
inbox, outbox = [], []
stack_ops = 0                 # every stack push or pop counts as 1

def push(x):
    global stack_ops
    inbox.append(x)
    stack_ops += 1

def pop():
    global stack_ops
    if not outbox:                         # refill ONLY when outbox is empty
        while inbox:                       # moving reverses the order:
            outbox.append(inbox.pop())     # the oldest item ends up on top of outbox
            stack_ops += 2
    stack_ops += 1
    return outbox.pop()

ops = [1, 2, 3, 0, 4, 0, 0, 0]             # a number = push it, 0 = pop
pushed = 0
for x in ops:
    if x != 0:
        push(x)
        pushed += 1
        print("push " + str(x))
    else:
        print("pop -> " + str(pop()))
print("Stack operations: " + str(stack_ops) + " for " + str(pushed)
      + " elements (at most 4 each = " + str(4 * pushed) + ")")
# Time: O(1) amortized per operation, O(N) worst case for one pop. Space: O(N).

followUps:
Because moving elements while out still holds older ones would bury those older elements under newer ones, and the queue would then hand items out in the wrong order.

out is correct only if everything in it is older than everything in in, with the oldest on top. A transfer into an empty out keeps that true; a transfer on top of existing elements breaks it.

Example: push 1, 2. Pop transfers both (out top is 1) and returns 1, leaving 2 in out. Push 3. If you now moved 3 across, it would sit on top of 2, and the next pop would return 3 instead of 2. Waiting until out is empty returns 2 first, then moves 3.

It also protects the cost proof: each element is moved exactly once, which is what gives O(1) amortized.

Not with the standard constructions: with plain FIFO queues, either push or pop costs O(N) every time, so you do not get the amortized O(1) that the two-stack queue enjoys.

The reason is that a queue never reverses order. Moving items from one stack to another flips them, which is what makes the two-stack trick cheap; moving items between queues keeps the same order, so reaching the newest item always means cycling past all the others.

The usual one-queue version makes push O(N) and pop O(1):

void push(int x) {
  q.offer(x);
  for (int i = 0; i < q.size() - 1; i++)
    q.offer(q.poll());   // rotate x to the front
}

Example: queue [2, 1] (front is 2), push 3 gives [2, 1, 3], two rotations give [3, 2, 1], so pop returns 3. Space O(N).

code.title: Sliding window maximum with a monotonic deque of indices
code.python:
from collections import deque

a = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7]
k = 3
dq = deque()        # indices; their values go down from front to back
out = ""

for i, x in enumerate(a):
    if dq and dq[0] <= i - k:
        dq.popleft()                  # front left the window
    # smaller-or-equal values at the back can never be a max again
    while dq and a[dq[-1]] <= x:
        dq.pop()
    dq.append(i)
    if i >= k - 1:
        out += " " + str(a[dq[0]])    # front = max of this window

print("Input:" + "".join(" " + str(x) for x in a) + ", k = " + str(k))
print("Window maximums:" + out)
# Time: O(N), each index enters and leaves the deque once.
# Space: O(k) live entries.

followUps:
Use a growing and shrinking window with two deques: one tracks the window's maximum (values going down), the other its minimum (values going up).

  1. Add a[r] to both deques, popping from the back as usual.
  2. While max - min > limit, move l right, and drop a deque's front if it holds index l.
  3. The answer is the largest r - l + 1 seen.
while (a[maxD.peekFirst()] - a[minD.peekFirst()] > limit) {
  if (maxD.peekFirst() == l) maxD.pollFirst();
  if (minD.peekFirst() == l) minD.pollFirst();
  l++;
}
best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);

Example [8, 2, 4, 7], limit 4: [8,2] has a gap of 6, so shrink; [2,4] is fine (length 2); [2,4,7] has a gap of 5, shrink to [4,7]. Answer 2. Time O(N), space O(N).

It appears whenever a DP value is built from the best of the previous K DP values, for example dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[i-K] ... dp[i-1]). That inner maximum is a sliding window maximum over the dp array itself.

Computed naively it costs O(N × K). Keeping a deque of indices whose dp values go down gives the window maximum at the front in O(1), so the whole DP is O(N).

Example (Jump Game VI): a = [1, -1, -2, 4, -7, 3], K = 2. dp becomes [1, 0, -1, 4, -3, 7]: for the last cell the window holds dp[3] = 4 and dp[4] = -3, the front is 4, so 3 + 4 = 7.

The same idea solves Constrained Subsequence Sum, the bounded knapsack speed-up, and Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K (a deque over prefix sums).

code.title: Evaluate an infix expression with two stacks (numbers and operators)

followUps:
Run the same two-stack algorithm, but make the operand stack hold tree nodes instead of numbers. Wherever the evaluator would compute a op b, you instead build a node.

  1. A number becomes a leaf node and is pushed.
  2. When an operator is applied: pop the right child, pop the left child, create Node(op, left, right) and push it.
  3. At the end the one node left on the stack is the root.
void apply() {
  Node r = nodes.pop(), l = nodes.pop();
  nodes.push(new Node(ops.pop(), l, r));
}

Example 3 + 4 * 2: * is applied first and builds (4 * 2); then + builds a root with left child 3 and right child that subtree. A post-order walk of the tree evaluates it (11) or prints postfix 3 4 2 * +. Building is O(N) time and space.

A minus sign is unary when there is nothing to its left that it could subtract from: it is the first token, or the previous non-space token is ( or another operator. If the previous token is a number or ), it is an ordinary subtraction.

Examples: in -3 + 5 and 2 * (-3) the minus is unary; in 5 - 3 and (1 + 2) - 3 it is binary. So keep one variable, the previous token, as you scan.

Two ways to handle it once detected:

  • Push a 0 first, turning -3 into 0 - 3. Simple, but wrong for 2 * -3, which would become 2 * 0 - 3.
  • Treat it as a separate operator (say ~) with the highest precedence that pops one number and pushes its negative. This is correct everywhere.

Detection is O(1) per token.

code.title: Iterative DFS with an explicit stack on a 100000-node chain (no stack overflow)
code.python:
n = 100000
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for i in range(n - 1):            # chain 0 - 1 - 2 - ... - 99999
    adj[i].append(i + 1)
    adj[i + 1].append(i)

# A recursive DFS here would need depth 100000; Python stops at about 1000
# (RecursionError), just like Java throws StackOverflowError.
seen = [False] * n
stack = [0]                       # a plain list on the heap, so depth is no problem
seen[0] = True
visited = 0
last = -1
while stack:
    u = stack.pop()               # same job as "enter the recursive call"
    visited += 1
    last = u
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not seen[v]:
            seen[v] = True        # mark when pushing: no duplicates
            stack.append(v)

print("Nodes in chain: " + str(n))
print("Visited with explicit stack: " + str(visited))
print("Last node reached: " + str(last))
# Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V) on the heap instead of one call frame per node.

followUps:
Push each node with a flag that says whether its children have already been handled. The first time you pop a node you put it back with the flag set and push its children; the second time you pop it, all its children are done, so you output it.

stack.push(new Object[]{root, false});
while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
  Object[] e = stack.pop(); Node n = (Node) e[0];
  if ((boolean) e[1]) { visit(n); continue; }
  stack.push(new Object[]{n, true});
  for (Node c : reversed(n.children)) stack.push(new Object[]{c, false});
}

Example: root 1 with children 2 and 3. Pops go 1 (re-pushed), 2 (re-pushed, no children), 2 visited, 3, 3 visited, 1 visited: output 2 3 1.

A shortcut for trees: do a pre-order that goes "node, right, left" and reverse the result. Both are O(N) time and O(N) space.

Because a stack hands things back in the reverse of the order you pushed them. Recursion takes the first neighbour in the list and dives into it straight away; the iterative version pushes all neighbours and then pops the last one first.

Example: node A has neighbours [B, C, D]. Recursive DFS visits A, B, ... Iterative DFS pushes B, C, D and pops D, so it visits A, D, ...

Both are valid depth-first orders, and anything that only needs reachability (counting components, finding any path) is unaffected. When the exact order matters, for example to match expected output or produce the smallest path, either push the neighbours in reverse order, or keep an iterator per node on the stack so each node resumes where it stopped.

A second difference: marking a node as visited when it is pushed, as opposed to when it is popped, can also change the order on graphs with cycles.

code.title: Spotting the clue: "days until warmer" is a next-greater problem (monotonic stack)
code.python:
temp = [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]
n = len(temp)
wait = [0] * n          # 0 = no warmer day ahead

# Clue: "for each day, how long until a warmer one" = next greater element.
# The brute force scans right from every day: O(N^2). The stack does it in O(N).
st = []                 # days still waiting for a warmer day
for i in range(n):
    while st and temp[st[-1]] < temp[i]:
        day = st.pop()
        wait[day] = i - day     # distance needs indices, not values
    st.append(i)

print("Temperatures:" + "".join(" " + str(x) for x in temp))
print("Days until warmer:" + "".join(" " + str(x) for x in wait))
# Time: O(N). Space: O(N).

followUps:
"Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K" (LeetCode 862), where the array may contain negative numbers. It reads like a classic shrink-from-the-left sliding window, but that window is wrong here.

The plain window relies on this: making the window longer only increases the sum. With negatives that fails. Example [2, -1, 2], K = 3: the window [2] is too small, [2, -1] is even smaller, and only the whole array reaches 3. Worse cases make the window shrink past the real answer.

The fix: build prefix sums P and keep a deque of indices with increasing P values. For each j, pop from the front while P[j] - P[front] >= K (recording j - front), and pop from the back while P[back] >= P[j] (a later, smaller prefix is always a better start). Time O(N), space O(N).

The end of the array is no longer the end of the search: elements at the back can be answered by elements at the front. The standard fix is to go around twice, using i % n to read values.

  • Monotonic stack (next greater in a ring): loop i from 0 to 2n - 1, push indices only when i < n. Example [1, 2, 1] gives [2, -1, 2]: the last 1 finds the 2 on the second lap.
  • Window problems: same doubling, but never let a window be longer than n, or you would count an element twice.
  • Maximum subarray sum in a ring: the answer is the larger of the normal best and total - (minimum subarray), with a special case when all numbers are negative.

The cost stays linear: O(2N) = O(N) time and O(N) space, with no need to actually copy the array.

code.title: Bounded blocking queue: a producer and a consumer with back-pressure
code.python:
import queue
import threading

CAPACITY, ITEMS, POISON = 3, 20, -1
# put() blocks when 3 items are waiting; get() blocks when the queue is empty
q = queue.Queue(maxsize=CAPACITY)
result = {"sum": 0, "count": 0}

def producer():
    for i in range(1, ITEMS + 1):
        q.put(i)                 # waits if the consumer is slow
    q.put(POISON)                # "no more work" marker

def consumer():
    while True:
        x = q.get()              # waits if nothing is ready
        if x == POISON:
            break                # clean shutdown
        result["sum"] += x
        result["count"] += 1

p = threading.Thread(target=producer)
c = threading.Thread(target=consumer)
p.start()
c.start()
p.join()
c.join()
print("Capacity " + str(CAPACITY) + ", producer sends 1.." + str(ITEMS))
print("Consumer received " + str(result["count"]) + " items, sum = " + str(result["sum"]))
# Time: O(1) per put/get. Space: O(capacity), never more than 3 items in memory.

followUps:
It is a fixed array used as a ring with two counters: tail, which only the producer changes, and head, which only the consumer changes. Because each counter has exactly one writer, no lock and no compare-and-swap is needed.

  1. Producer: if tail - head == capacity the buffer is full; otherwise write buf[tail & mask], then publish tail + 1.
  2. Consumer: if head == tail it is empty; otherwise read buf[head & mask], then publish head + 1.

The capacity is a power of two, so & mask replaces the slower %. Example with capacity 4: head = 5, tail = 7 means 2 items, in slots 1 and 2.

Two details make it correct and fast: the counters must be volatile (or written with lazySet) so the other thread sees a slot only after it is filled, and they are padded apart to avoid false sharing. Both operations are O(1).

Put a special "stop" item, the poison pill, into the queue after the last real item. A consumer that takes it knows there is no more work and leaves its loop. Because the pill travels through the queue in order, everything queued before it is still processed.

static final Task POISON = new Task();
// producer, when finished:
queue.put(POISON);
// consumer:
while (true) {
  Task t = queue.take();
  if (t == POISON) break;
  process(t);
}

Rules: compare with == against one shared object; with N consumers send N pills (or have each consumer put the pill back before exiting); with several producers, send the pills only after all producers are done.

Example: 3 consumers, 100 tasks: enqueue the 100 tasks, then 3 pills. Alternatives are ExecutorService.shutdown() plus awaitTermination, or interrupting the threads.

code.title: Differential test: monotonic stack vs brute force on random arrays with duplicates
code.python:
seed = 1

def rnd():
    # tiny repeatable random generator
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 75 + 74) % 65537
    return seed

# the solution under review: next strictly greater element, O(N)
def fast(a):
    res = [-1] * len(a)
    st = []
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while st and a[st[-1]] < x:
            res[st.pop()] = x
        st.append(i)
    return res

# the obviously correct version: scan right from every index, O(N^2)
def brute(a):
    res = [-1] * len(a)
    for i in range(len(a)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(a)):
            if a[j] > a[i]:
                res[i] = a[j]
                break
    return res

tests = 300
mismatches = 0
for _ in range(tests):
    n = 1 + rnd() % 8
    a = [rnd() % 5 for _ in range(n)]      # small values force duplicates
    if fast(a) != brute(a):
        mismatches += 1

print("Arrays: length 1..8, values 0..4 (many duplicates)")
print("Random tests run: " + str(tests))
print("Mismatches: " + str(mismatches))
# Time: O(tests * N^2) because of the brute force. Space: O(N).

followUps:
Generate many small random arrays, run both the fast solution and a brute force on each, and stop at the first array where they disagree, printing it.

Random r = new Random(42);
for (int t = 0; t < 10000; t++) {
  int[] a = r.ints(1 + r.nextInt(8), 0, 5).toArray();
  if (!Arrays.equals(fast(a), brute(a)))
    throw new AssertionError(Arrays.toString(a));
}

Why these choices matter:

  • Short arrays (length 1 to 8): a failing case is small enough to trace by hand.
  • Tiny value range (0 to 4): forces duplicates, which is where strict versus non-strict bugs hide. Values up to 109 would almost never repeat.
  • Fixed seed (42): the same failure shows up again on the next run.

Example: a version that pops on <= fails on [2, 2] within the first few tests. Cost: 10000 × O(N2) with N at most 8, which runs in milliseconds.

The most common bug is treating equal values the same way on both sides, which counts some subarrays twice or not at all. Each element should own the subarrays where it is the minimum, and with duplicates exactly one of the equal elements must own each subarray.

The rule: use a strict comparison on one side and a non-strict one on the other, for example "previous smaller" (stop at <) and "next smaller-or-equal" (stop at <=).

Example [2, 2]: the subarrays are [2], [2], [2,2], so the answer is 6. Strict on both sides lets both 2s claim [2,2] and gives 8. Non-strict on both sides lets neither claim it and gives 4. The samples usually have no duplicates, so this slips through.

The runner-up bug is overflow: a[i] * left * right must be computed in long and reduced modulo 109 + 7.
